Neonates of Fusconaia cuneolus emerge after a brief incubation at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], with eclosion occurring approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] after fertilization. The resulting glochidia, which are the parasitic larval stage characteristic of unionid mussels, measure just 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] in shell length at birth, a diminutive size that reflects the energetic constraints of lecithotrophic development. Upon successful encystment on a suitable fish host and subsequent metamorphosis, the juveniles drop off and settle into the substrate. At the moment of settlement and metamorphic climax, the young bivalves exhibit a shell length of 0.03 centimeters , marking the onset of the post-metamorphic juvenile stage when they begin filtering phytoplankton from the water column. This transition from a parasitic to a free-living existence represents a critical bottleneck in the species' life history. The exceptionally small size of both the glochidia and the newly settled spat predisposes them to high mortality from predation and physical disturbance, meaning that recruitment success is heavily dependent on the availability of stable, low-energy microhabitats within the riverbed.

As the juvenile bivalves grow, they gradually transition from newly settled recruits into sub-adults. Growth in shell length is rapid during the first few years, but it decelerates markedly as the animal approaches its upper size limit. Based on extensive surveys of adult specimens from the species' restricted range in the upper Tennessee River drainage, the maximum shell length attained by Fusconaia cuneolus is approximately 9 centimeters [Li = approximately 9 centimeters]. This ultimate shell length is relatively modest compared to other members of the subfamily Ambleminae, many of which can exceed 12 or even 15 centimeters. The asymptotic size is thought to be constrained by the energetic costs of maintaining physiological function in the cool, oligotrophic streams this species inhabits. In terms of body mass associated with this size limit, individuals at 9 centimeters in shell length carry a total wet weight that approaches 26 grams [Wwi = 26 grams], a value that was estimated by correcting for the dimensions of a congener, Unio tumidus. This relatively low mass for a given shell length suggests a lean body condition, likely reflecting the low food availability characteristic of headwater streams.

Reproductive activity in Fusconaia cuneolus begins only after a prolonged juvenile period, with puberty occurring when individuals reach a shell length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This size threshold is typically not attained until approximately 20 years of age, based on von Bertalanffy growth model fitting to size-at-age data from mark-recapture studies. Reaching this critical size of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters] in shell length marks the onset of gametogenesis, when the gonads first become active and the animal begins diverting resources toward reproductive effort. The delay in reaching this reproductive milestone is substantial, reflecting the slow growth rates and high metabolic costs of living in the cool, oligotrophic conditions of the species' native habitat. It is also worth noting that the size at puberty shows relatively little variation across the population, suggesting strong genetic or energetic canalization. Once this size threshold is crossed, however, individuals enter a reproductively active phase that can last for several decades, during which they produce gametes annually as long as water temperatures and food resources remain favorable.

Fecundity in mature Fusconaia cuneolus is remarkably high, reflecting an life-history strategy that compensates for the extremely high mortality rates experienced by the parasitic larval stage. Gravid females release their glochidia into the water column during the summer months, with the reproductive season typically coinciding with water temperatures around 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. At this temperature, a single female of standard shell length 6.3 centimeters produces approximately 310 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 310 offspring per day], a figure derived from direct counts of glochidia released from captive individuals over a 24-hour period. This daily reproductive output is substantial and translates into an enormous total annual fecundity. The high number of glochidia produced each day is thought to be an adaptation to the very low probability of any individual larva successfully encountering a compatible fish host, encysting, and completing metamorphosis. Only a tiny fraction of the millions of glochidia released by a single female over her lifetime will ever survive to settlement, making this high reproductive rate a critical component of population persistence.

Longevity data for Fusconaia cuneolus indicate that this species is among the longest-lived of the North American unionid mussels. Field surveys consistently reveal the presence of old, heavily eroded individuals, and the maximum lifespan in natural populations is estimated to be 12,775 days [am = 12,775 days] under a thermal regime centered on 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This corresponds to approximately 35 years, although some researchers, such as Bauer in 1987, have reported that typical natural populations can contain individuals exceeding 93 years of age. The discrepancy between the 35-year estimate and the 93-year observation likely reflects differences in the thermal history of the rivers studied, as growth and senescence rates are strongly temperature-dependent in bivalves. At colder temperatures, the metabolic rate is depressed, which can slow the accumulation of cellular damage and extend lifespan. This extreme longevity, combined with the late age at puberty and high fecundity, classifies Fusconaia cuneolus as an archetypal slow-lived, equilibrium species, highly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbance because of its low intrinsic rate of population increase.
